venues.d: The white colonial grande dame the whole city is measured against — and still the finest room in it.
A Norman Foster-restored colonial estate in the rainforest — resort calm, minutes from the city.
A glass pavilion on the water, looking straight across the bay to the skyline.

venues.n: The Paiza Collection at Marina Bay Sands
venues.d: The private hotel-within-the-hotel at Marina Bay Sands — arrival by Rolls-Royce, a dedicated lift, total discretion.
Raffles' all-villa resort debut — private pools and hilltop calm, the marque's newest Singapore address.
The surest hands off Orchard Road — quiet, art-filled, and effortless with families.
A fan-shaped tower with the group's quiet precision and rooms that fan out over the bay.
A serious art collection and octagonal-window bathtubs framing the bay — grand, and quietly famous for it.
Old-world St. Regis grandeur off Orchard — butler service and a museum's worth of art in the halls.
A polished, freshly reimagined Orchard tower — central, capable, and easy on the shopper.
The three-towered icon crowned by the ship-shaped SkyPark — the photograph the whole world knows.
A dependable, art-hung tower by the convention halls — spacious and unshowy.
A calm, design-led newcomer off Orchard — vertical greenery and quiet good taste.
The famous hotel-in-a-garden — cascading sky terraces of greenery over the old town.
The grand old General Post Office, a neoclassical landmark reborn at the mouth of the river.
Two restored 1930s landmarks turned into a small, characterful house in the civic heart.
Peranakan shophouse charm woven into a grand hotel, over the arts-and-heritage quarter.
A soaring atrium tower with wide bay views and a smooth, Asian-service ease.
A big, capable twin-tower house with one of the city's best spas attached.
A garden-set heritage landmark of 1900, long a favourite for its quiet lawns and durian pastries.
A high-energy design resort by the marina — for members who want the music turned up.
Julien Royer's modern French inside the National Gallery — the city's most decorated table.
A French institution since 1994 — classical haute cuisine and one of Asia's great cellars.
Björn Frantzén's Singapore house — Scandinavian purity meets Japanese finesse across three floors of a shophouse.
Rishi Naleendra's precise, fermentation-led cooking — Sri Lankan soul, exacting technique.
'Reinventing British' cooking on the 70th floor — technique and a view in equal measure.
Sun Kim's highwire act between Korea and Europe — inventive, assured, quietly thrilling.
Emmanuel Stroobant's French-Asian cooking, waterside, with the bay for a backdrop.
An eight-seat sushi counter flown daily from Toyosu — the quietest luxury in town.
Spice-spiked modern Indian cooking that earned Singapore's most exciting two-star climb.
A serene Edomae counter, newly promoted — precise, unhurried, deeply traditional.
Tetsuya Wakuda's intimate multi-room dinner at Marina Bay Sands — Japanese-European, jewel-like.
Everything through the custom four-tonne ovens — the barbecue counter that became a pilgrimage.
The world's first Michelin-starred Peranakan kitchen — Malcolm Lee's refined Nyonya cooking.
Han Liguang's 'new Singaporean' cooking — hawker memories reimagined with local farms.
Kevin Wong's ode to Nusantara flavours — Malay-archipelago cooking with real elegance.
Jason Tan's 'gastro-botanica' — vegetable-led fine dining of great delicacy.
Wolfgang Puck's modern steakhouse — the city's most polished room for a great cut.
Refined Cantonese in a garden-pavilion setting — the grand Chinese lunch, immaculately done.
Third-generation Szechuan mastery — mapo tofu the way it should be.
A long-running critical darling — European cooking with a wine list to match.
Ivan Brehm's 'crossroads cooking' — a thoughtful blur of world cuisines under one star.
Louis Han's memory-led Korean cooking — seasonal, personal, quietly moving.
A warm, family-run Italian doing quietly excellent contemporary cooking.
European fine dining with a light, generous hand in a garden-hotel setting.
Classic, exacting Cantonese — the grand hotel Chinese dinner at its most assured.
Teochew cooking done with rare precision — braised goose and clear, clean flavours.
A Cantonese stalwart in the Chijmes cloisters — dim sum and roast meats, done properly.
Contemporary Australian-French cooking in a restored chapel-precinct room.
A refined Latin-American tasting menu — precise, warm and hard to book.
Malcolm Lee's second act — Southeast-Asian heritage cooking with a green conscience.

venues.n: Hill Street Tai Hwa Pork Noodle
venues.d: The bak chor mee that holds a Michelin star — proof a single hawker bowl can be world-class.
Modern Sri Lankan cooking with real fire and spice — hoppers and curries done with care.
Bold, herb-driven Thai cooking that punches well above its price.
A legendary Hainanese chicken rice house, freshly promoted for doing the classic best.
A Hong Lim hawker favourite, newly starred by the Bib for its wanton mee.
A famed hawker plate of Hokkien mee — smoky, wet, and quietly perfect.

venues.n: Sin Heng Claypot Bak Koot Teh
venues.d: Peppery pork-rib soup in a claypot — old-Singapore comfort, credentialed by the inspectors.
A beloved kway chap stall — braised, soulful, and worth the queue.
Clean, restorative Teochew fish porridge — the antidote to a heavy week.

venues.n: Lao Fu Zi Fried Kway Teow
venues.d: Char kway teow with real wok hei — the smoky char that defines the dish.
Fragrant coconut-rice nasi lemak done with a cook's care — a Bib-listed favourite.
Singapore's best bar, and among Asia's finest — a cocktail room the world flies in for.
Cocktails that tell Singapore's own story — local flavours, world-class craft.
A sustainability-minded bar in the Chijmes cloisters — inventive, and quietly conscientious.
Regional Southeast-Asian spirits and foraged flavours — a bar with a real sense of place.

The Supertree Grove, the Cloud Forest with the world's tallest indoor waterfall, and the record-holding Flower Dome — a garden built like a city. Come at dusk to walk the OCBC Skyway between the Supertrees, then stay for the free Garden Rhapsody light-and-sound show at night. Wide, flat and pram-friendly, so it works well for a multi-generation group.

venues.n: Marina Bay Sands SkyPark Observation Deck
venues.d: The ship-shaped deck cantilevered 57 storeys up gives the definitive Singapore skyline view — the bay, the CBD towers and Gardens by the Bay laid out below. Go at golden hour; if you are staying at the hotel you get the famous 150m infinity pool, which non-guests cannot access.

venues.n: Singapore Botanic Gardens & National Orchid Garden
venues.d: Singapore's only UNESCO World Heritage Site and the world's first tropical botanic garden on the list — 82 hectares of rainforest, lakes and heritage trees in the middle of the city. The ticketed National Orchid Garden holds 1,000+ species, including the hybrids named for visiting heads of state. Free entry to the wider gardens; ideal for an unhurried morning walk.

The lotus-shaped building beside Marina Bay Sands, best known for the permanent teamLab 'Future World' immersive digital installations that children and adults get equally lost in. It also runs serious travelling exhibitions on science, design and art.

The world's largest public collection of modern Southeast Asian art, housed in the beautifully restored former Supreme Court and City Hall. Worth it for the architecture alone; finish with a drink at the rooftop bar for a Padang-and-bay view. Strong for collectors and anyone who wants depth beyond the theme parks.

venues.n: Merlion Park & the Marina Bay waterfront promenade
venues.d: The half-lion, half-fish icon spouting water into the bay, with the classic straight-on view of Marina Bay Sands across the water. The best move is simply to walk the full bayfront loop — Merlion to Esplanade to the Helix Bridge to Sands — especially after dark when everything is lit.

venues.n: Chinatown & Sri Mariamman Temple / Buddha Tooth Relic Temple
venues.d: Restored shophouse lanes, the ornate Sri Mariamman (Singapore's oldest Hindu temple) and the grand red-and-gold Buddha Tooth Relic Temple within a few streets of each other. Wander Pagoda and Temple Streets, then eat at Chinatown Complex or Maxwell. Plenty of vegetarian and South Indian food nearby, which helps veg and Jain travellers.

The most decorated hawker centre in the city — eight stalls landed in the 2025 Michelin Bib Gourmand list. Home of the legendary Tian Tian Hainanese chicken rice; go early, eat like a local, and understand why Singaporeans take food this seriously.

The old Malay-Arab quarter — the golden-domed Sultan Mosque, textile and perfume shops on Arab Street, and Haji Lane, a narrow alley of boutiques, murals and rooftop bars. The most atmospheric quarter to wander on foot in the late afternoon.

The most sensory neighbourhood in Singapore — garland stalls, spice shops, the colourful Tan Teng Niah house and the vivid Sri Veeramakaliamman Temple. For Indian travellers it is both familiar and a revelation; some of the best vegetarian thalis and dosas in the city are here, and Tekka Centre downstairs is a proper wet-market-plus-hawker experience.

Southeast Asia's Universal park, with zones themed to Jurassic World, Transformers, Sci-Fi City and more — the anchor family attraction on Sentosa. Book Express passes to skip the queues; combine with a Sentosa hotel night to avoid a rushed day.

One of the world's largest aquariums, with a vast Open Ocean tank you can sit in front of like a cinema, home to manta rays and sharks. Reliable, air-conditioned and genuinely calming — an easy win with young children or grandparents.

The world's first nocturnal wildlife park — you ride a tram through dimly lit habitats to see lions, tapirs and Asian elephants active after dark. A distinctive Singapore evening; opens at 6:30pm, so pair it with the neighbouring parks earlier in the day.

Consistently rated among the world's best zoos for its open, moated 'rainforest' design — famous for the Breakfast with Orangutans experience. Adjoining River Wonders adds giant pandas and a huge freshwater collection. The strongest single day out for families with children.

Asia's largest bird park, with eight walk-through aviaries you can stroll through as free-flying birds swoop around you, and 3,500 birds across 400 species. The newest of the Mandai parks and beautifully designed — quieter and more contemplative than the zoo.

Singapore's oldest housing estate — curved 1930s Art Deco blocks, an indie bookshop, third-wave cafés and the excellent Tiong Bahru Market for hawker breakfast. The city's most walkable, low-key morning: no ticket, just wander and eat.

The heart of Peranakan Singapore — rows of pastel shophouses with ornate ceramic tiles, and the celebrated Koon Seng Road terraces. Come for laksa and kaya toast, and to see a heritage quarter that won a UNESCO Asia-Pacific conservation award. Off the tourist trail and all the better for it.

A jewel-box museum devoted to Straits-Chinese culture — beadwork, porcelain, jewellery and the material world of the Peranakans, recently reopened after a full revamp. The best primer before wandering Katong or Emerald Hill.

The country's oldest museum, telling the Singapore story from its trading-port origins through independence, in a grand colonial building with a striking glass rotunda. A good orientation on day one — note the History Gallery is under restoration until late 2026, but the rest remains open.

A 9km chain of hilltop parks linked by walkways, crowned by Henderson Waves — Singapore's highest pedestrian bridge, a sculptural timber wave 36m up with harbour and skyline views. Do the shorter Mount Faber to HortPark stretch for the best of it; the bridge is lit at night.

The city's green lung — boardwalks over the reservoir, monkeys and monitor lizards, and a 250m suspension bridge strung through the rainforest canopy. A proper jungle hike ten minutes from downtown; go early to beat the heat.

A hilltop park layered with history — 14th-century royal grounds, WWII bunkers and the famous 'Tree Tunnel' spiral staircase that fills every Instagram feed. A shaded, central green break between museum visits.

A single, quiet cul-de-sac of exquisitely preserved Peranakan terrace houses tucked just off the Orchard Road shopping strip — a five-minute detour that most visitors miss. Have a drink at one of the old shophouse bars at the foot of the hill.

Singapore's mile of malls — ION Orchard, Ngee Ann City / Takashimaya and Paragon carry the full luxury roster. Efficient, air-conditioned and comprehensive; the practical choice when you want the brands under one roof rather than a hunt.

venues.n: The Shoppes at Marina Bay Sands
venues.d: The waterfront luxury mall with 170+ premium brands, a canal you can ride a sampan on, and the Apple 'floating' store on the bay. High-end flagship shopping with the Sands spectacle attached — and a rain-proof link to the museum, casino and hotel.

The grand colonial hotel where the Singapore Sling was invented in 1915 — restored to full lustre, with an arcade of luxury boutiques and the Long Bar where you still drop peanut shells on the floor. Worth a walk-through and a cocktail even if you are not staying.

A restored 19th-century convent and Gothic chapel turned into a courtyard of restaurants and bars — one of the prettiest places in the city for a candlelit dinner. A polished, atmospheric evening away from the malls.

The riverside strip of old godowns (warehouses) now full of restaurants and bars, and the departure point for the classic bumboat river cruise past the Merlion to Marina Bay. Do the cruise at dusk for the city lights; the nightlife here has just been refreshed.

A gorgeous Victorian cast-iron market hall — a national monument — packed with hawker stalls, where the neighbouring street closes each evening to become the smoky 'Satay Street'. The most convenient CBD hawker experience and a beautiful building in its own right.

Singapore's largest hawker hub — 700+ stalls over several floors, including the stall that once held a Michelin star for soya-sauce chicken. Gritty, authentic and endlessly cheap; go with an empty stomach and no plan.

A gloriously eccentric 1930s park of lurid dioramas illustrating Chinese mythology — most famously the graphic 'Ten Courts of Hell'. Free, strange and unforgettable; nothing else in the city is remotely like it.

Singapore's oldest Hindu temple, its rainbow gopuram tower crowded with painted deities rising incongruously out of Chinatown. During the annual Theemithi festival, devotees walk over hot coals in the courtyard. A moving, active place of worship — for Indian travellers, a piece of home in an unexpected setting.

The city's oldest and most important Hokkien temple, built in 1839 by grateful immigrants where the sea once lapped the shore — an exquisite piece of southern-Chinese architecture on Telok Ayer Street. Pair it with the mosque and church on the same historic street of faiths.

The giant observation wheel over the bay, with 30-minute rotations that reveal the skyline, the Formula 1 street circuit and, on a clear day, Malaysia and Indonesia. You can book a private capsule with dinner for a discreet celebration.

venues.n: Jewel Changi Airport & the HSBC Rain Vortex
venues.d: The world's tallest indoor waterfall thundering seven storeys through a glass dome ringed by rainforest — and it is inside the airport. Worth a deliberate visit even without a flight; a genuinely jaw-dropping arrival or departure, and a fine last few hours before you fly.

A 15-minute bumboat from Changi Point drops you into Singapore of the 1960s — a rustic island of last-remaining kampong (village) life, mangroves and jungle you explore by rented bicycle. The Chek Jawa wetlands at low tide are extraordinary. The city's easiest escape into another era.

venues.n: Palawan Beach & the Southern Ridges of Sentosa
venues.d: Sentosa's family beach, with a rope suspension bridge out to the 'Southernmost Point of Continental Asia' and a lookout tower. Low-key, shaded and easy — a gentler counterpoint to the island's theme parks.

The 'durian'-domed performing arts centre on the bayfront — world-class concerts, theatre and a strong run of free performances on the outdoor stage most evenings. Check the programme; there is nearly always something on, much of it free.

venues.n: Singapore Cable Car (Mount Faber to Sentosa)
venues.d: A glass cabin gliding from a rainforest hilltop across the harbour to Sentosa, with the port, container ships and Southern Islands spread below. The most scenic way to reach the island; private-cabin dining is available for a special occasion.

A cluster of restored 1930s colonial army barracks turned contemporary-art enclave — commercial galleries, artist studios and a relaxed café or two under old rain trees. The quiet, serious end of the Singapore art scene, and pleasantly uncrowded.

Singapore's only preserved coastal fort, with WWII gun emplacements and tunnels and a treetop 'Skywalk' out to the ramparts. A substantial, breezy history stop on Sentosa that balances out the theme-park day.

A rugged, deliberately undeveloped nature park on the northeast coast — coastal forest, casuarina groves and quiet beaches, best explored on foot or by bike. One of the last genuinely wild-feeling corners of Singapore, and rarely busy.

A one-hour ferry from Tanah Merah reaches Bintan's beach resorts and spas — the standard Singapore beach escape for a day or an overnight. A useful reset when the city gets intense; passport and visa-on-arrival apply, so plan the paperwork.
Across the causeway lies Malaysia — cheaper spa days, seafood, and Legoland Malaysia for younger children, all doable as a day trip. Weekday mornings avoid the border crush; keep passports handy.

A dam-turned-park with a grassy rooftop that is the city's favourite kite-flying and sunset picnic spot — and a rare uncrowded, front-row view straight across the water to the Marina Bay skyline. Quietly one of the best free things to do at dusk.

venues.n: Kranji countryside & Sungei Buloh Wetland Reserve
venues.d: The rural far northwest — mangrove boardwalks alive with migratory birds, mudskippers and the occasional estuarine crocodile, plus a scatter of hydroponic and goat farms. An unexpectedly wild, agricultural side of Singapore that almost no visitor sees.
The city's defining cocktail room — polished, unhurried, and among the best on earth.
An Art Deco cathedral to gin — a 15-metre tower of 1,300 labels beneath a soaring 1930s ceiling.
Cocktails that tell Singapore's own story — local flavours, world-class craft.
Regional spirits and foraged flavours — a bar with a real, rooted sense of place.
A hand-built shophouse bar of upcycled charm — six classics, remade weekly from the market.
Vinyl on the turntable, pan-Asian plates and drinks — the easy, low-lit end of world-class.
An agave den hidden in plain sight — tequila and mezcal handled with real seriousness.
A sustainability-minded bar in the Chijmes cloisters — inventive, and quietly conscientious.
A new entrant that arrived straight into the ranks — precise, confident, worth the seat.
A grand-hotel bar with real craft behind it — the polished nightcap done properly.
The New York speakeasy's Singapore outpost — showman bartending and a room that runs late.
Above the National Gallery, staring down the Padang to the bay — the city's finest rooftop terrace.
Fifty-seven floors up on the SkyPark — the definitive high-above-the-bay drink.
A rooftop pool bar at the water's edge — the softer, quieter front-row seat to the skyline.
